questions.question: What is strong consistency?

options.text: After a write completes, all subsequent reads see that write—linearizable behavior

questions.explanation: Strong consistency: once write acknowledged, all readers see it immediately. System behaves as if there's one copy. Requires coordination (consensus, locks). Higher latency, lower availability during partitions.

questions.question: What is eventual consistency?

options.text: Given no new updates, all replicas will eventually converge to the same value

questions.explanation: Eventual consistency: replicas may temporarily diverge, but will converge if updates stop. Allows higher availability and lower latency. Reads might see stale data. Common in distributed systems.

questions.question: What is the CAP theorem relationship to consistency models?

options.text: During network partition, must choose between strong consistency (CP) or availability (AP with eventual consistency)
You can have all three always

questions.explanation: CAP: during partition, choose C or A. Strong consistency (CP): reject writes/reads if can't confirm. Eventual consistency (AP): accept operations, reconcile later. Tradeoff is fundamental.

questions.question: When would you choose strong consistency?

options.text: Financial transactions, inventory management, anything where incorrect data causes serious problems

questions.explanation: Strong consistency for: bank transfers (can't double-spend), inventory (can't oversell), booking systems (can't double-book). Where incorrectness has real consequences. Accept latency/availability tradeoffs.

questions.question: When would you choose eventual consistency?

options.text: Social media feeds, product reviews, analytics, DNS—where temporary staleness is acceptable

questions.explanation: Eventual consistency for: social feeds (seeing post 1 second late is fine), product reviews, view counts, DNS, caching. Where availability and performance matter more than immediate accuracy.

questions.question: What is read-your-writes consistency?

options.text: A user always sees their own writes, even if other users might see stale data

questions.explanation: Read-your-writes: after you write, you see your write. Others might not yet. Weaker than strong consistency, stronger than eventual. Important for user experience—your actions should be reflected.

questions.question: What is monotonic read consistency?

options.text: Once you read a value, subsequent reads won't return older values
Reading one record at a time

questions.explanation: Monotonic reads: time doesn't go backward for a client. If you see version 5, you won't later see version 4. Prevents confusing 'time travel'. Achievable with session stickiness or version tracking.

questions.question: How does DynamoDB handle consistency?

options.text: Configurable per-request: eventually consistent reads (default, faster) or strongly consistent reads

questions.explanation: DynamoDB: choose per read. Eventually consistent: might be stale, lower latency, half the cost. Strongly consistent: guaranteed current, higher latency, full cost. Flexibility to optimize per use case.

questions.question: What is the latency impact of strong consistency?

options.text: Higher latency—must wait for coordination/consensus across replicas before responding

questions.explanation: Strong consistency latency: writes must reach quorum/all replicas, reads may need to check multiple replicas. Cross-region: even worse (100s of ms). Eventual consistency: respond from nearest replica immediately.

questions.question: What is causal consistency?

options.text: Operations that are causally related are seen in the same order by all nodes

questions.explanation: Causal consistency: if A causes B, everyone sees A before B. Concurrent operations (no causal relation) can be seen in different orders. Stronger than eventual, weaker than strong. Good middle ground.

questions.question: What is the 'stale read' problem in eventual consistency?

options.text: Reading outdated data because replication hasn't propagated the latest write yet

questions.explanation: Stale reads: write to replica A, read from replica B before replication. B returns old value. Duration depends on replication lag. Mitigations: read-your-writes, sticky sessions, version checks.

questions.question: An e-commerce site shows product inventory. Which consistency model and why?

options.text: Eventual consistency for display, strong consistency for purchase

questions.explanation: Hybrid approach: display inventory with eventual consistency (fast, scalable, slight staleness OK). At checkout, use strong consistency (prevent overselling). Match consistency to business requirements.
